title: Song choices and Sleepytime Down South as theme
summary: Randolph says Armstrong simply liked the Southern-flavored songs, not a managed image, recalls the press reaction to his Yes, Lord and notes Sleepytime as his theme.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Listening to the tunes, the words of the tunes that Louis was singing, several of them, like Dusky Stevedore, That's My Home, Cabin in the Pines -- That's My Home was a different session, but what Louis was doing, the type of tunes he was doing then -- was somebody trying to build his image with the public as a homesick black Southerner? So many of these Down on the levee type of things --
Yeah, he -- Louis just liked it. Louis liked it. I know the press jumped on Louis about something,
when he made "Sleepytime Down South," and he says, "Yes, Lord," and they jumped on it because he made an expression like that.
"Sleepytime Down South," that was Louis Stevens, of course. Did he select it as a theme or did it just work out that way, or was it such a popular record that it became the theme song?
He selected it as a theme, but that's -- he had an arrangement on that, "Sleepytime Down South." That's the one where I had -- oh, this is a different band, though.
That was the earlier band. The '31 band.
Right, yeah, but -- yes, but he kept that up. Then I'll tell you about that one when we get to this band, because this -- we're still talking about -- what, the '34 band?
